cards.q: Largest dental distributor in the world?
cards.a: Henry Schein — roughly 40% of the market. #1.
cards.n: Your notes spell it "Henry Shine."

cards.q: Who are the Big 3 distributors, in order?
cards.a:
1. Henry Schein (~40%)
  2. Patterson
  3. Benco
cards.n: Notes say "Banko" — it's Benco.

cards.q: What role does the distributor play in a dental office?
cards.a: The quarterback — everything the office runs on comes through them.

cards.q: How are dental distributor reps typically employed?
How does Henry Schein get devices to the office?
cards.a: Ships all dental devices straight to the door.

cards.q: Roughly how many dentist products are out there?
Who are the largest dental manufacturers?
cards.a: Envista, Dentsply Sirona, Straumann.
cards.n: Notes: "In Vista / Dens Supply Cerona / Sventum."

cards.q: Which implant companies does Henry Schein own?
cards.a: BioHorizons and Camlog — its implant arm.
cards.n: Straumann is the big independent implant player.

cards.q: Which two companies sell dental equipment and technology?
cards.a: A-dec and Planmeca.
cards.n: Notes: "Plan Mecha."

cards.q: Newest way to take x-rays?
cards.a: The intraoral scanner.

cards.q: Why do dentists think about money differently than surgeons and physicians?
cards.a: Surgeons and physicians are on salary. Dentists make what they charge their patients — so every purchase is their own money.

cards.q: What is dental insurance really?
cards.a: Not insurance — more of a discount program.

cards.q: How does Medicaid work in dental?
cards.a: It doesn't. Medicaid covers the uninsured and people on welfare on the medical side; dental has no equivalent.

cards.q: Which procedures are normally out of pocket?
cards.a: Dentures, crowns, veneers.

cards.q: Roughly how many dentists are there in the world?
What do the letters DMD after a name tell you?
cards.a: A typical dentist — a general practitioner.

cards.q: Name the dental specialists.
cards.a:
• Orthodontists
  • Endodontists
  • Pedodontists
  • Periodontists
  • Oral surgeons

cards.q: Biggest clear aligner company in the game?
cards.a: Invisalign.
cards.n: Notes: "Invisilin."

cards.q: What are the Big 4 procedure categories?
cards.a:
1. Implants
  2. Preventives
  3. Restoratives
  4. Endodontics

cards.q: Maxilla — what is it, and what's its one job?
cards.a: The upper jaw. Softer ground. Supports the upper teeth — and the sinus is right nearby.

cards.q: Mandible — what is it, and what's its one job?
cards.a: The lower jaw. Stronger ground. Supports the lower teeth and contains an important nerve.

cards.q: Gingiva — what is it, and what's its one job?
cards.a: The gums. A protective seal. Keeps bacteria away and protects the tooth and bone.

cards.q: Alveolar bone — what is it, and what's its one job?
cards.a: The foundation. Holds the tooth — and shrinks if the tooth is lost.
cards.n: That shrinking is why bone grafts get sold alongside implants.

cards.q: Trace the structure from the jaw out to the tooth.
cards.a: Jaw bone (maxilla or mandible) → alveolar bone → gums → teeth.

cards.q: Incisors, canines, premolars, molars — what does each one do?
cards.a:
1. Incisors — cut
  2. Canines — tear
  3. Premolars — crush
  4. Molars — grind

cards.q: Are teeth bone? Do they grow back?
cards.a: No and no. Teeth aren't bone. Enamel is the hardest substance in the body, but once it's lost the body can't rebuild it.
cards.n: Your notes say teeth are the hardest bone and the only bone that regenerates — both are wrong, and a dentist will catch it. The fact that enamel can't come back is what sells fluoride, sealants and restoratives.

cards.q: Why bother learning tooth composition at all?
cards.a: So you can talk about products that interact with each layer — that's the whole point of the anatomy.

cards.q: Cavities — what does the dentist buy?
cards.a:
1. Composite filling
  2. Bonding agents
  3. Caries detection devices
  4. Fluoride
  5. Sealants

cards.q: Periodontal disease — what does the dentist buy?
cards.a:
1. Ultrasonic scalers
  2. Hand scalers
  3. Lasers
  4. Bone grafts
  5. Antimicrobials

cards.q: Crooked teeth — what does the dentist buy?
cards.a:
1. Braces
  2. Clear aligners
  3. Temporary anchoring devices (TADs)
  4. Orthognathic surgery, in severe cases

cards.q: Losing teeth — what does the dentist buy?
cards.a:
1. Implant systems
  2. Bone grafts
  3. Dentures
  4. Digital dentures
  5. Implant components

cards.q: What are your odds the dentist is actually available when you walk in?
cards.a: About a 30% hit rate.

cards.q: How many touches before you get consistent calls?
Dentists are very ___ driven.
cards.a: Promo and sell driven.

cards.q: How do you build a relationship in this business?
cards.a: Show up. Be consistent. Bring value.

cards.q: Three things that keep a dentist calling you back?
cards.a:
1. Consistency
  2. Follow up
  3. Say what you'll actually do

cards.q: What matters most in dental sales?
cards.a: Relationships. They're the major thing.

cards.q: How many incisors, and where?
cards.a: 8 — 4 upper, 4 lower. Central and lateral.
cards.n: Single root, thin edge. Built for cutting.

cards.q: How many canines, and what else are they called?
cards.a: 4 — the "cuspids" or "eye teeth".

cards.q: How many premolars, and what else are they called?
cards.a: 8 — the "bicuspids".
cards.n: Bi-cuspid = two cusps. That's literally the name.

cards.q: How many molars?
cards.a: 12 — or 8 once the wisdom teeth come out.

cards.q: Which teeth have the longest roots in the mouth?
cards.a: Canines.
cards.n: Which is why they're very stable and the last teeth to be lost.

cards.q: How many cusps does a molar have?
cards.a: 3 to 5, with 2–3 roots. The largest teeth in the mouth.

cards.q: When do the first molars come in?
cards.a: Around age 6 — that's why they're called the "6-year molars".

cards.q: Where do premolars sit, and what do they do?
cards.a: Between the canines and molars. They're the transition — chewing and grinding. One or two roots.

cards.q: The team analogy for the four tooth types?
cards.a:
1. Incisors — skilled forwards (finesse, visible, aesthetic)
  2. Canines — anchors (stability, guidance)
  3. Premolars — midfielders (transition, support)
  4. Molars — power players (heavy lifting, most force)
cards.n: Straight from the training. Handy if you need to explain teeth to a patient.

cards.q: Which jaw has denser bone?
cards.a: The mandible — densest in the mouth, especially at the front. The maxilla is less dense.
cards.n: Density drives almost everything else: implant stability, how fast teeth move.

cards.q: Which jaw moves teeth faster in orthodontics, and why?
cards.a: The maxilla — thinner bone means faster movement. The lower jaw is slower.

cards.q: What's inside the maxilla that matters for implants?
cards.a: The maxillary sinuses.
cards.n: Not enough bone between the sinus and the mouth means a sinus lift before an upper back implant.

cards.q: What shape is the mandible, and what runs through it?
cards.a: Horseshoe shaped, with the mental foramen — the nerve exit — sitting between the premolars.

cards.q: What does healthy gingiva look like?
cards.a: Pink, stippled, and it doesn't bleed.
cards.n: Diseased: red, swollen, bleeds easily. Stippled means a slight orange-peel texture.

cards.q: What is gingiva made of?
cards.a: Keratinized tissue around the teeth — free gingiva and attached gingiva.

cards.q: What happens to alveolar bone once a tooth is gone?
cards.a: It resorbs — the bone disappears because nothing is stimulating it.
cards.n: "Use it or lose it." This one fact drives ridge preservation grafts, immediate placement, and half the implant conversation.

cards.q: How much bone can be lost after a tooth comes out?
cards.a: 40–60% in the first three years.
cards.n: Which is why timing matters so much — wait too long and there's nothing left to place an implant into.

cards.q: What actually causes a cavity?
cards.a: Streptococcus mutans + sugar → acid, and the acid demineralizes enamel.

cards.q: How does decay progress?
cards.a: White spot → enamel caries → dentin caries → pulp involvement.
cards.n: Catch it at the white spot and it's preventive. Let it reach the pulp and it's a root canal.

cards.q: Caries Class I and II?
cards.a:
Class I — pits and fissures on chewing surfaces.
Class II — between the back teeth.

cards.q: Caries Class III, IV and V?
cards.a:
Class III — between the front teeth.
Class IV — front teeth involving the corner or edge.
Class V — at the gumline.
cards.n: Class VI is cusp tips.

cards.q: What are healthy gums, by the numbers?
cards.a: 1–3mm pocket depth, no bleeding on probing, no bone loss.

cards.q: Gingivitis vs periodontitis?
cards.a:
Gingivitis is reversible — gums inflamed, bleeding, but no bone loss yet.
Periodontitis is irreversible — 4mm+ pockets and bone loss visible on x-ray.
cards.n: The line between them is bone loss. Once bone is gone it doesn't come back on its own.

cards.q: What causes gingivitis?
cards.a: Plaque accumulation. It's reversible at this stage.

cards.q: Angle's Class I?
cards.a: Normal molar relationship — but with crowding, spacing or other issues. The most common.

cards.q: Angle's Class II?
cards.a: Lower jaw too far back relative to the upper — overbite/overjet, the "buck teeth" look.
cards.n: Division 1: front teeth protrusive. Division 2: front teeth retroclined.

cards.q: Angle's Class III?
cards.a: Lower jaw too far forward — underbite. Can be dental or skeletal, and it's the hardest to treat.

cards.q: Partial vs complete edentulism?
cards.a:
Partial — missing some teeth. Bridges, partial dentures, implants.
Complete — no teeth in the arch. Complete dentures, implant-supported dentures, All-on-4.
cards.n: Partial edentulism gets sorted by Kennedy Classification (I–IV) based on where the gaps are.

cards.q: What happens to someone after they lose teeth?
cards.a: Bone resorption, bite collapse, facial aging, functional impairment.
cards.n: It's not just cosmetic — the face structurally changes as the bone goes.

cards.q: Why do incisors matter commercially?
cards.a: They're the most visible teeth, so aesthetics are critical — shade matching for composites, bonding and veneers, and aligner cases often focus here.
cards.n: Also trauma-prone in contact sports, which matters if the practice sees athletes.

cards.q: Why are canines strong implant candidates?
cards.a: Bone volume. They're also critical for "canine guidance" in the bite and strategic in denture and partial design.
cards.n: An impacted canine means complex orthodontic treatment.

cards.q: Why are premolars often extracted?
cards.a: To create space for orthodontic treatment.
cards.n: They're also a common site for cracked tooth syndrome, and implant-friendly locations.

cards.q: Why do molars drive so much product?
cards.a: Highest decay rate — grooves and pits mean sealants. Most common location for crowns, most complex root canal anatomy, and implants there need more bone because the forces are higher.

cards.q: Which teeth are usually impacted or extracted?
cards.a: Wisdom teeth — #1, 16, 17 and 32.

cards.q: Where's the best place to put an implant, and why?
cards.a: The mandible — dense bone. It also supports implant-retained dentures well.
cards.n: Upper back implants are harder: sinus lifts, slower stability, tougher for immediate load.

cards.q: What product category does the mandibular nerve create?
cards.a: Imaging. Nerve management is critical down there, so the practice needs to see exactly where it runs before placing.

cards.q: What sells off gum disease?
cards.a: Soft tissue lasers, periodontal instruments, grafting materials for recession, and tissue management during impressions.

cards.q: Two product names worth knowing?
cards.a:
DIAGNOdent — caries detection.
Arestin — local antimicrobial for perio.

cards.q: When does a ridge preservation graft get placed?
cards.a: At extraction — before the bone has a chance to resorb.
cards.n: Implants help maintain bone too. That's the argument for immediate placement.

cards.q: What's the ROI pitch on periodontal maintenance?
cards.a: Perio maintenance patients are recurring revenue for the practice.
cards.n: Selling the business case, not just the product.

cards.q: What's the biggest opportunity area, and why?
cards.a: Edentulism — the population is aging and the baby boomers are hitting peak tooth-loss years.
cards.n: Implant systems, bone grafting, dentures, digital denture workflow.

cards.q: Three questions to actually open with?
cards.a:
1. "What percentage of your restorations are composite vs amalgam these days?"
  2. "What percentage of your Class II cases do you treat with aligners vs traditional braces?"
  3. "The baby boomers are hitting peak tooth-loss years — how is your practice positioned to capture this?"
cards.n: Straight from the training. Each one gets a dentist talking about their own practice instead of your catalog.

questions: Largest dental distributor in the world?
Three names, three slots: Schein, Patterson, Benco. Schein alone is roughly the other two put together.
Roughly what share of the market does Henry Schein hold?
Close to half of everything a dental office orders moves through one company. That's why every Big 3 conversation starts with Schein.
Patterson is the one in the middle - big enough to compete with Schein head-on, which is why they show up against you.
Benco is the smallest of the Big 3 and family-owned. It's the one people forget - and the one your notes had as "Banko."
The distributor is the ___ of a dental office.
A quarterback never scores, but nothing moves until they touch it. Same job: you don't do the dentistry, but everything they use came through you.
How are dental distributor reps mostly employed?
W-2 means these are employees with territories, not gig contractors. It's a career track, and it's why the company invests in training you.
Roughly how many dentist products are out there?
Nobody memorizes 300,000 SKUs - not you, not the dentist. That gap is exactly why they need a rep they trust instead of a catalog.
Which two companies sell dental equipment and technology?
A-dec and Planmeca sell the big hardware - chairs, units, imaging. Different world from consumables: bought rarely, costs a fortune, lasts a decade.
The intraoral scanner is the digital replacement for goopy impressions and film. If an office is buying one, they're modernizing - that opens other doors.
Which implant companies does Henry Schein own?
Schein doesn't just ship other people's implants, it owns two implant brands. Distributor and manufacturer at the same time.
Who are the largest dental manufacturers?
Manufacturers make it, distributors move it. Dentsply Sirona builds the product; Schein puts it on the doorstep. Don't mix the two lists up.
Roughly how many dentists are there in the world?
200,000 worldwide is a small, closed profession. Reputations travel - which is why burning one office actually costs you.
Dental insurance is really more of a:
It's a discount program with an annual cap, usually around ,,000-$2,000. Patients blow through that fast, and everything after is cash out of pocket.
How does Medicaid work in dental?
It doesn't - there's no dental equivalent
The medical safety net just doesn't extend here. No equivalent program means the patient pays or the work doesn't happen.
Which of these is normally out of pocket?
Dentures, crowns and veneers are the high-ticket items insurance barely touches. That's where the case-acceptance conversation lives.
Why does a dentist treat every purchase as personal money?
They make what they charge their patients
The dentist usually owns the practice. Surgeons and physicians draw a salary; a dentist takes home what's left. Every box you sell comes out of their own pocket - price it like you know that.
What does DMD after a name tell you?
DMD or DDS both mean general dentist - the degrees are equivalent. Specialists carry an additional title on top.
Biggest clear aligner company in the game?
Invisalign is the category - people say it the way they say Kleenex. Note the spelling: Invis-align, as in aligning.
Which one is NOT a dental specialist?
The dental specialties: perio (gums), endo (root canals), pedo (kids), ortho (straightening), oral surgery. Cardiology is not on the list.
What are the Big 4 procedure categories?
Implants, preventives, restoratives, endodontics. Learn these as buckets - almost every product you sell drops into one of them.
Front to back, food gets broken down in stages: cut, tear, crush, grind. Incisors are the front blades that start it.
Canines are the pointed ones - think of a dog's fang. Made for tearing, and they have the longest roots in the mouth.
Premolars sit between the tearers and the grinders, and they do the in-between job: crushing.
Molars are the flat millstones at the back. Cut, tear, crush, grind - grinding is the last step before you swallow.
MAXilla = MAX, at the top. It's fixed to the skull and doesn't move.
The mandible is the one that actually moves - your lower jaw is the only bone in your skull with a real joint.
Gingiva is gums - same root as gingivitis, which is literally inflamed gums.
What sits right next to the maxilla?
The sinus sits directly above the upper back teeth. That's why upper implants sometimes need a sinus lift first - there isn't enough bone between.
The inferior alveolar nerve runs through the lower jaw. Hit it and the patient loses feeling in their lip - which is why lower implants get scanned and planned so carefully.
What is the alveolar bone's one job?
Holds the tooth - and shrinks if it's lost
It holds the tooth, and it shrinks once the tooth is gone because nothing is stimulating it anymore. That shrinkage is the entire reason bone grafts get sold alongside implants.
Order it from the jaw out to the tooth:
Jaw bone, alveolar bone, gums, teeth
Gums, jaw bone, teeth, alveolar bone
Teeth, gums, alveolar bone, jaw bone
Alveolar bone, jaw bone, teeth, gums
Work outward from the deepest structure to the one you can see: jaw bone, alveolar bone, gums, teeth.
Are teeth bone, and do they grow back?
Not bone, but they do grow back
Bone has a blood supply and heals; enamel has neither, so damage is permanent. That one fact is why the entire preventive category - fluoride, sealants, restoratives - exists.
Cavities - what does the dentist buy?
Composite filling, bonding agents, fluoride, sealants
Match the product to the problem. Cavities are a restore-and-prevent job: fill what's decayed, then seal and strengthen what isn't.
Periodontal disease - what does the dentist buy?
Perio is a gum and bone problem, so the tools clean below the gumline and rebuild what was lost - scalers, lasers, grafts, antimicrobials.
Crooked teeth - what does the dentist buy?
Straightening runs cheapest to most invasive: braces, aligners, TADs for tough cases, and surgery only when the jaw itself is off.
Losing teeth - what does the dentist buy?
Replacing teeth means replacing the foundation too - which is why grafts sell next to implants. Remember the alveolar bone shrinks once the tooth is gone.
A temporary anchoring device is a mini screw placed as a fixed anchor point to pull teeth against. Temporary - it comes out when the move is done.
Odds the dentist is actually available when you walk in?
Roughly two out of three stops won't get you face time. Plan the route expecting that, and treat the staff as the real relationship.
How many touches before you get consistent calls?
6 to 8. Most reps quit around three and conclude the office isn't interested - the ones who keep going get the calls.
They respond to promos and deals. Lead with what's actually on offer, not a general check-in.
What keeps a dentist calling you back?
Consistency, follow up, doing what you said
Consistency, follow up, and doing what you said you'd do. Cheapest price wins one order; being reliable wins the account.
Central and lateral incisors, top and bottom. Single root, thin edge, built for cutting.
One at each corner of the arch. Also called cuspids or eye teeth.
Also called bicuspids. Bi-cuspid = two cusps, which is literally where the name comes from.
How many molars, wisdom teeth included?
Drops to 8 once the wisdom teeth come out - which is most people.
Which teeth have the longest roots in the mouth?
Longest roots means most stable, which is why canines are the last teeth to be lost.
What does "bicuspid" tell you about a premolar?
Bi = two, cuspid = cusp. The name describes the chewing surface.
How many cusps does a molar have?
Largest teeth in the mouth, 2-3 roots, and the most complex anatomy to work on.
When do the first molars erupt?
They're literally called the 6-year molars. First adult teeth in, and often the first to decay.
In the team analogy, what are the canines?
Incisors are the forwards (visible, aesthetic), premolars the midfielders (transition), molars the power players (heavy lifting).
Which jaw has the densest bone?
Densest at the front of the lower jaw. That density is why it's the best implant location.
Where do teeth move faster in orthodontics?
Thinner maxillary bone moves faster; the dense mandible is slower. Same reason implants behave differently up top.
Why do upper back implants often need a sinus lift?
The maxillary sinus leaves too little bone
The nerve is in the way
Sinus sits right above the upper back teeth. Not enough bone between them means grafting first - which is a sale.
Between the premolars in the lower jaw
In the roof of the mouth
It's where the nerve exits the mandible. Knowing it's there is why imaging gets sold with lower implants.
What do healthy gums look like?
Stippled means a faint orange-peel texture. Diseased gums are red, swollen and bleed easily.
What happens to alveolar bone when a tooth is lost?
Use it or lose it - nothing is stimulating the bone anymore. This is the single most useful fact in implant selling.
How much bone can be lost in the first 3 years after tooth loss?
That speed is why immediate placement and ridge preservation grafts matter - wait and there's nothing to place into.
Strep mutans plus sugar makes acid
Bacteria plus sugar makes acid, acid demineralizes enamel. That's the whole disease process.
Caught at the white spot it's preventive. Reaching the pulp means a root canal - and a very different product list.
Class I caries are found where?
Pits and fissures on chewing surfaces
Class I is the classic sealant target - the grooves on top of molars.
Class V caries are found where?
Class II is between back teeth, Class III between front teeth, Class IV a front corner or edge, Class VI cusp tips.
The probe number is the whole diagnosis. 4mm+ with bone loss is periodontitis.
Gingivitis is gums only and reversible. Once bone is lost it's periodontitis, and that doesn't reverse.
Periodontitis starts at what pocket depth?
4mm+ plus bone loss on the x-ray. Chronic is slow, aggressive is rapid.
Lower jaw too far back - overbite
The buck-teeth look. Division 1 has the front teeth sticking out, Division 2 has them tipped back.
Lower jaw too far forward - underbite
Hardest of the three to treat, and the one most likely to need orthognathic surgery.
Which malocclusion class is most common?
Normal molar relationship, but with crowding or spacing. Most aligner cases live here.
What are the options for complete edentulism?
Partial edentulism gets bridges, partials or implants - and is sorted by Kennedy Classification I-IV.
What happens to someone after losing teeth?
Bone resorption, bite collapse, facial aging
The face structurally changes as bone disappears. It's a functional problem, not a cosmetic one.
Most visible - shade matching, bonding, veneers
Aesthetics drive the sale up front. Also trauma-prone in contact sports, which matters for practices seeing athletes.
Why are molars the sealant and crown category?
Highest decay rate from grooves and pits
Grooves trap food and bacteria. Molars also take the most force, so they crack and get crowned most often.
The upper back, behind the sinus
Dense bone means stability. It also supports implant-retained dentures well.
Pulling premolars makes room to straighten the rest. They're also a common cracked-tooth site.
Arestin is the other name worth knowing - a local antimicrobial for periodontal pockets.
When does a ridge preservation graft go in?
Get ahead of resorption. Bone disappears fast once the tooth is gone, so the graft goes in the same visit.
What's the ROI pitch on periodontal maintenance?
It's recurring revenue for the practice
Sell the business case, not just the product. Perio patients come back on a schedule, forever.
What makes edentulism the big opportunity?
An aging population hitting peak tooth loss
It only affects a few patients
Baby boomers are hitting peak tooth-loss years. Implants, grafts, dentures, digital denture workflow - all of it.
Which is an actual conversation opener from the training?
"What percent of your restorations are composite vs amalgam?"
"Can I speak to whoever does the ordering?"
Good openers get the dentist talking about their own practice instead of your catalog.
